newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open weaker in quiet trading.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open weaker in quiet trading.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened slightly weaker in quiet trade on Tuesday after the release of economic data indicating moderate inflationary pressures in the U.S. economy, analysts said.
The U.S. Department of Commerce reported June retail sales rose 0.5 percent compared to a downwardly revised 0.3 percent decline in May.
A Reuters survey had forecast a 0.2 percent rise in sales and a 0.5 percent increase minus the automobile component.
"The market traded off initially on fears of a bad number and overseas selling," said a trader with a Canadian bank.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill weakened to yield 3.20 percent from 3.18 percent at Monday's close. The three-month cash T-bill fell to yield 3.18 percent.
Activity was light in the Canadian money market this morning with many accounts absent and trading largely dealer driven.
"We're seeing nothing. No account flows," the trader said.
Analysts said the likelihood of another Bank of Canada interest rate hike was continuing to weigh on prices.
The central bank raised interest rates 25 basis points three weeks ago in an effort to cushion the Canadian dollar.
"It (T-bill market) is still going to remain under pressure because of the generally negative sentiments in the market," the trader added.
Economic reports which will be closely watched by the market include Canada's consumer price index for June out on Thursday, and Friday's merchandise and wholesale trade data.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill dropped to yield 3.47 percent from a 3.42 percent yield at Monday's close. The one-year T-bill softened to yield 4.12 percent from 4.09 percent.
The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 3.25 percent, the center of the Bank of Canada's 3.0-3.5 percent target range.
